newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Prebble says politics not sole brake on RBNZ.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Prebble says politics not sole brake on RBNZ.

text.p: Act New Zealand leader Richard Prebble said his impression after receiving a briefing from the Reserve Bank on Wednesday was that political uncertainty was not the only factor preventing it from easing monetary policy in the face of a rising dollar.
Prebble told Reuters a centre-left government would not find things as easy as it expected

"Our talks were in confidence and we didn't ask questions that they couldn't answer. Having said, that it is abundantly obvious the political situation does make it harder for the RB to take action, mainly because it makes it harder for the market to make rational decisions."

Economic nationalist New Zealand First holds the balance of power after the October 12 election and has begun talks with both the main opposition Labour Party and the caretaker National Party government on coalitions.
But Prebble, whose radical free-market party has eight MPs and has offered its support to National, said there were other reasons the RBNZ was not acting now.
"I think the RB still wants to be reassured inflationary pressures in the economy are under control."
He said it was a shame Labour had not talked to Treasury about the effects of its spending plans.

"It is abundantly obvious that if they were to attempt those spending promises, interest rates would rise instantly and much higher than people appreciate, and that will have a devastating effect on the dollar and the export sector," Prebble said.
He said Labour's policy to delay next year's proposed second round of tax cuts would help.

"Treasury by law will have to give in December its forecast of the effects of a new government's programme and that's going to be read very quickly by the markets and a left-wing government will find that its programme is unsustainable almost immediately."
Prebble told journalists that Wednesday's three-hour meeting between the coalition negotiating teams from National and New Zealand First was good news for National.
"My prediction is that Mr Peters isn't going to side with either party. The moment he sides with either he will lose about a third of his supporters," Prebble said.
"My prediction is that we will end up with a minority National government because that doesn't require anyone to make a decision, and that always wins."
